analysis.one_liner: Requires automakers to sell a rising share of zero-emission vehicles, reaching all-electric by 2040.
analysis.headline: The Zero-Emission Vehicles Act attracted 26 Democratic sponsors but never received a committee vote or a floor vote in the House before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Clean Air Act to set a national zero-emission vehicle standard. Starting in 2030, each carmaker would have to deliver a rising percentage of zero-emission vehicles for sale in the US — 50% in 2030, 75% by 2035 — and from 2040 onward could sell only zero-emission passenger cars. Carmakers that fell short would have to buy zero-emission credits from carmakers that exceeded their quota, pay a civil penalty worth twice the value of the missing credits, or face a manufacturing injunction after 2040. States would keep their power to set stricter rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who breathe the air: the bill targets tailpipe emissions of pollutants and greenhouse gases nationwide, with the full benefit arriving over the 2030s as the sales mandate ramps up. Makers of electric and fuel-cell vehicles would gain a new revenue stream selling compliance credits to lagging competitors, and electric utilities would gain charging demand. The bill also explicitly preserves states' authority to set their own stricter zero-emission rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone breathing cleaner air; electric-vehicle makers

how_it_helps.text: Sets a firm national schedule — 50% zero-emission sales in 2030 rising to 100% in 2040 — replacing the patchwork of state rules with a single nationwide requirement [S2] [S3].
Creates a tradeable credit market so carmakers that sell more electric vehicles than required can sell credits to those that sell fewer, and requires a public annual report on the market [S3].

Backs the mandate with real teeth: civil penalties equal to twice the value of missing credits, deposited into the Highway Trust Fund, and after 2040 EPA can enjoin manufacture of any non-zero-emission passenger vehicles [S2] [S3].
Preserves the ability of states and local governments to adopt their own emissions and zero-emission vehicle standards without being preempted [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers whose sales remain concentrated in gasoline vehicles would bear compliance costs — buying credits or paying civil penalties — which would likely be passed into new-car prices. Buyers of new gasoline cars during the transition, and drivers of used gas cars facing fuel and maintenance costs, would pay in the near term. The oil industry would lose gasoline demand as the mandate ramps up.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gas-vehicle automakers, new-car buyers, oil industry

drawbacks.text: The mandate would raise the cost of new cars during the transition: carmakers that fall short must buy credits or pay a penalty equal to twice the credits' value, costs likely passed to buyers [S3].

The schedule is aggressive — 50% of sales zero-emission by 2030 — and the bill's answer to consumer-choice concerns is only a nonbinding 'sense of Congress' that manufacturers should diversify models, leaving affordability and charging access to be worked out elsewhere [S3].

Because the bill locks in a credit-trading system, electric-vehicle leaders like Tesla would collect credit revenue from slower competitors, a cost embedded in the price of every gasoline car sold rather than borne directly by Congress [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's aim — eliminating tailpipe emissions from new passenger cars by 2040 — addresses air pollution and climate change at national scale, and its penalties are strong enough to matter. The honest costs are real: compliance costs land on new-car buyers during the 2030s, the 50%-by-2030 start is faster than most voluntary industry plans, and near-term consumer choice in vehicle types narrows. Whether it is a good deal depends on weighing those transition costs against avoided pollution and fuel costs over decades; the bill itself offers no consumer-cost relief or charging-infrastructure funding, which is its biggest design gap.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Environment and Climate Change subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Levin (D-CA) introduced the bill with Rep. Joe Neguse on May 15, 2019 [S1].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and the next day to the Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change [S5].
Twenty-five House Democrats joined as cosponsors; no Republican signed on [S4].
The action history shows no further action — no subcommittee vote, no full committee markup, no floor vote — through the end of the 116th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers that sell gasoline vehicles are better off: they face no sales mandate, no credit purchases, and no civil penalties. The oil industry keeps unrestricted gasoline demand, and the status quo of state-by-state rules continues.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gasoline-vehicle automakers and the oil industry

industries.note: The bill would force them to convert sales to zero-emission vehicles on a fixed schedule or buy credits and pay penalties, costs likely passed into new-car prices. Their interest in blocking or weakening the mandate runs against the public's interest in cleaner air.

industries.industry: Electric and fuel-cell vehicle makers (e.g., Tesla)
industries.note: The bill creates a national tradeable credit market in which EV sales generate credits they can sell to lagging competitors, converting clean-vehicle leadership into a permanent revenue stream. Their business interest aligns with the bill's clean-air goal.
A 100%-zero-emission sales requirement from 2040 would steadily shrink gasoline demand. The industry's interest in blocking the bill runs against the public's interest in lower tailpipe emissions.
A large national EV fleet means growing electricity demand and charging infrastructure business. Their interest runs alongside the public's clean-air interest.
